$comment: Moved from apps/landing/src/lib/architecture.json (the landing's /architecture page now redirects here). Corrected on 2026-10-30: 10 MCP tools, Cardano account at sign-up, envelope accepted live, x402 on Cardano; added the seller, Masumi escrow and registry, and the receipt verifier.

nodes.label: AI agent
nodes.what: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Grok, connected as an MCP client. It can read balances and ask for payments, but it can never sign anything.
nodes.why: ZyroPay is built so agents can pay on a user's behalf, while every payment still goes through the policy engine.
nodes.guarantee: The agent's token only ever maps to its own agent id, and its tools can only create requests, never signatures.

nodes.label: ZyroPay app
nodes.what: The iOS and Android app (with a web build) where people sign up, see their portfolio, send and receive, approve agent payments and manage agents.
nodes.why: It is the only place where the user's passkey is used, so every human approval happens here.
nodes.guarantee: Approvals are signed with the passkey on the device, and the review shown must match the exact transaction the server checks.

nodes.label: Your passkey
nodes.what: A passkey on the user's device that proves it is really them. It is the only root of their Turnkey sub-organization.
nodes.why: Being non-custodial means only the user can move their funds on their own, so the passkey is the one root credential and ZyroPay holds none.
nodes.guarantee: Every approval needs a fresh passkey stamp; a session key stamp is accepted only for read-only queries.

nodes.label: Turnkey Auth Proxy
nodes.what: A Turnkey service that creates the passkey, the user's sub-organization and a default wallet at sign-up, with no ZyroPay backend involved.
nodes.why: It lets sign-up happen directly between the app and Turnkey. Turnkey documents that it has no access to funds.
nodes.guarantee: Its root layout is not documented, so the API checks the sub-org's root quorum on first login and refuses anything other than the user alone.

nodes.label: Turnkey parent org
nodes.what: ZyroPay's organization in Turnkey. It sits above every user's sub-organization.
nodes.why: The API needs to read a user's sub-org (for example to check its root quorum and mirror wallets), but should never be able to change it.
nodes.guarantee: The parent organization can read sub-orgs but cannot write to them.

nodes.label: Your Turnkey sub-org
nodes.what: A separate Turnkey organization for each user that holds their wallets and keys inside Turnkey. The user's passkey is its only root user.
nodes.why: Root actions in Turnkey bypass policies, so ZyroPay keeps itself out of the root quorum entirely.
nodes.guarantee: There is no ZyroPay root user, so no ZyroPay system can move funds on its own. ZyroPay also has no recovery override.

nodes.label: Delegated signer
nodes.what: An optional non-root key user inside the sub-org, used only for Autonomous mode. The user's own passkey creates it.
nodes.why: Autonomous payments need a signer without a human in the loop. It does not exist until the user turns on Autonomous for an agent.
nodes.guarantee: Its private key is stored encrypted, it is never in the root quorum, and revoking it destroys the key at once. In Always Ask, ZyroPay can sign nothing.

nodes.label: Turnkey policy envelope
nodes.what: Rules inside Turnkey that limit what the delegated signer may sign: allowed chains, allowlisted recipients, per-transaction caps and allowed programs.
nodes.why: A second, coarser line of defence that holds even if the ZyroPay API itself is compromised.
nodes.guarantee: A fully compromised API still cannot exceed the per-transaction envelope or pay a non-allowlisted recipient.

nodes.label: MCP server
nodes.what: A Cloudflare Worker that exposes 10 tools to AI clients (8 wallet and payment tools plus 2 read-only Masumi registry tools) and turns each tool call into one internal API call.
nodes.why: It keeps agents away from keys and data: it holds no Turnkey credentials, no database URL and no user session.
nodes.guarantee: It never signs. Results are sanitized and wrapped as untrusted data, and a compromised MCP worker can only create requests that still need approval or stay within limits.

nodes.label: Agent sign-in (OAuth)
nodes.what: The OAuth 2.1 authorization server inside the MCP worker. It shows a short code that the user approves in the app.
nodes.why: Agents need their own revocable access that is tied to one agent and approved by the user's passkey session.
nodes.guarantee: PKCE is required for every client, redirect URIs must match exactly, tokens are opaque and stored only as hashes, access tokens last 15 minutes by default, and revocation cuts off every token for an agent.

nodes.label: ZyroPay API
nodes.what: The system of record, running on Cloudflare Workers. It handles sessions, policy checks, the request state machine, spending reservations, Turnkey forwarding, broadcast, webhooks and audit.
nodes.why: One place enforces every rule, and it forwards the user's signed requests to Turnkey without being able to change them.
nodes.guarantee: The API never holds a user's root credential, validates every input with Zod, and fails closed when something is missing or unexpected.

nodes.label: Policy engine
nodes.what: Checks every agent payment against the agent's rules and returns allow, require approval or deny.
nodes.why: Turnkey cannot enforce USD limits, daily or monthly totals or per-agent rules, so those live here.
nodes.guarantee: New agents start in Always Ask with spending disabled and zero limits. A missing price, or an error during evaluation, never auto-allows a payment. Swaps and Cardano are never autonomous.

nodes.label: Request state machine
nodes.what: Tracks every payment request from creation to its final outcome through a fixed set of states.
nodes.why: An explicit transition table makes it impossible to skip a step, such as signing without a policy check.
nodes.guarantee: Illegal transitions throw, and an approval moves to SIGNING before Turnkey is called, so a duplicate approve can never sign twice.

nodes.label: Payload hash binding
nodes.what: A SHA-256 fingerprint of the payment's terms: network, from, to, asset, amount, fee cap, plugin, tool, nonce, expiry and idempotency key.
nodes.why: It ties an approval to exactly what the user saw, so nothing material can change after they approve.
nodes.guarantee: Any material change produces a new hash and the old approval no longer applies. The stamped body must also be byte-equal to the reviewed transaction.

nodes.label: Neon Postgres
nodes.what: The database for users, wallets, agents, policies, payment requests, approvals, spending reservations, the spending ledger, webhook events and audit logs.
nodes.why: Spending limits need an exact, shared record of what has been spent and what is reserved, even under concurrent requests.
nodes.guarantee: Agent requests run under a row lock and limits count spent plus reserved, so many requests at once can never jointly exceed a limit. Tokens are stored only as hashes.

nodes.label: Price sources
nodes.what: Provide USD prices used to value payments and portfolios.
nodes.why: USD limits need a valuation, and Turnkey has no price oracle.
nodes.guarantee: Values are rounded up, and a stale, unknown or failed price counts as no valuation, which never auto-allows a payment.

nodes.label: Job queue
nodes.what: A Cloudflare Queue that runs background steps: autonomous signing, broadcast, confirmation polling, push notifications, webhook processing and revocation retries.
nodes.why: Slow or retryable work runs outside the request, with retries and a dead-letter queue.

nodes.label: Scheduled sweeps
nodes.what: A Cron Trigger that runs every minute to expire old requests and re-check stuck ones.
nodes.why: A request waiting for approval should not stay open forever, and stuck broadcasts need a retry path.
nodes.guarantee: Requests past their expiry that have not started signing move to EXPIRED and their reserved spend is released.

nodes.label: Transaction builders
nodes.what: Build the unsigned transaction for Solana, EVM chains and Cardano from the payment terms, and simulate it before review.
nodes.why: ZyroPay builds the exact bytes the user reviews, using Turnkey sign-only so nothing is filled in after review.
nodes.guarantee: Fees are capped by the fee cap inside the payload hash, and a Solana transaction that is about to expire is rebuilt without changing the payload hash.

nodes.label: Independent decoder
nodes.what: Decodes the transaction bytes on its own, without network access, and checks they match the approved payment.
nodes.why: It catches any mismatch between what was approved and what is about to be signed or sent.
nodes.guarantee: It fails closed. A signed transaction that does not match the reviewed bytes fails the request before broadcast.

nodes.label: Broadcasters
nodes.what: Send the signed transaction to the network through ZyroPay's own RPC providers.
nodes.why: One broadcast and confirmation path for every chain family, instead of Turnkey sign-and-send.
nodes.guarantee: The transaction hash is stored before sending, and a rebroadcast re-sends the same bytes.

nodes.label: Confirmation tracker
nodes.what: Checks on chain whether a transaction is pending, confirmed, failed, expired or replaced.
nodes.why: The final outcome of a payment is decided by the chain, read through ZyroPay's own RPC.
nodes.guarantee: On confirmation the reserved spend is settled into the ledger once; on failure it is released.

nodes.label: Chain RPC providers
nodes.what: The node providers ZyroPay uses to read balances and history and to broadcast: Helius for Solana, Alchemy for Ethereum and Base, Blockfrost for Cardano.
nodes.why: Each provider is bound to one network, so mainnet and testnet are never mixed.
nodes.guarantee: Providers refuse any other network, the API checks genesis hash or chain id, and it never falls back to a public RPC.

nodes.label: Payment plugins
nodes.what: Adapters for swaps and paid web requests: Jupiter swaps on Solana mainnet, and x402 payments (Cardano preprod end to end; EVM and Solana signed but not handed off).
nodes.why: They let agents do more than plain transfers, with the same quote, binding and decode checks.
nodes.guarantee: Swaps are never autonomous. x402 on EVM and every Cardano payment always need the passkey.

nodes.label: Provider webhooks
nodes.what: Incoming notifications from Helius, Alchemy and Transak about chain activity and on-ramp orders.
nodes.why: They speed up updates, but are never the only source of truth.
nodes.guarantee: Signatures are checked on the raw body, duplicates are ignored, and events are reconciled with ZyroPay's own RPC reads before any state change.

nodes.label: Push notifications
nodes.what: Expo push messages that tell the user an approval is waiting or a payment landed.
nodes.why: Always Ask needs to reach the user quickly, without leaking payment details.
nodes.guarantee: Pushes carry no amounts or addresses and deep link only to a fixed set of screens in the user's own app, which then reloads everything from the API.

nodes.label: Error monitoring
nodes.what: Optional Sentry error reporting for the API, the MCP worker and the app. Nothing is sent until a DSN is configured.
nodes.why: Debugging needs error types and stack traces, but never secrets or personal data.
nodes.guarantee: Every event is scrubbed and fails closed: bodies, headers, user data, tokens, keys, recovery phrases, emails and IP addresses are removed, and no traces are sent.

nodes.label: x402 seller (example)
nodes.what: Cardano Address Intelligence: a paid data API on Cloudflare Workers that answers 402 with x402 v2 requirements (exact scheme, cardano:preprod) and runs the official @x402/cardano facilitator in-process. A second one, Token Intelligence, sells token reports.
nodes.why: ZyroPay needs a real third-party seller to pay. It is a separate party: it never sees a ZyroPay credential.
nodes.guarantee: Settlement happens only when the handler answers below 400, so a Blockfrost failure returns 503 and the buyer is not charged.

nodes.label: Masumi escrow
nodes.what: The canonical Masumi payment-v2 vested_pay script (Plutus V3) on Cardano. It holds a payment until the seller submits a result hash and the unlock time passes, or refunds it.
nodes.why: Paying a stranger up front needs a way to get the money back if nothing, or the wrong thing, is delivered.
nodes.guarantee: ZyroPay locks only into the canonical deployment and binds the exact datum bytes into the payload hash; the user's refund spends are passkey-signed.

nodes.label: Masumi registry
nodes.what: A permissionless registry of agents: each is a CIP-25 NFT under the V2 registry policy whose metadata names its endpoint and price.
nodes.why: An agent can find sellers, and ZyroPay can check that a seller claiming an identity really holds it.
nodes.guarantee: Registration proves identity binding, not trustworthiness. ZyroPay verifies a claimed identity on chain at quote time and refuses on any failure.

nodes.label: Delivery receipt verifier
nodes.what: Checks the seller's Ed25519 signature over the exact bytes the agent received, the paid URL, payTo and the payment transaction.
nodes.why: A paid response alone proves nothing about who sent it or whether it was altered.
nodes.guarantee: Only the holder of the paid address's key can produce a receipt that verifies; the MCP worker hashes the body itself, never trusting the seller's hash alone.

stateMachine.notes: A request is created, policy-checked, then either waits for the user (PENDING_APPROVAL) or is approved outright, and moves through SIGNING and BROADCAST to CONFIRMED. A deny ends in REJECTED, the expiry sweep moves CREATED, POLICY_CHECK, PENDING_APPROVAL and APPROVED requests to EXPIRED, and only requests that have not started signing can be CANCELLED; once signing starts, only the chain decides the outcome.

steps.text: You create a passkey on your phone when you sign up.
The app asks Turnkey's Auth Proxy to set up your account, with no ZyroPay server involved.
Turnkey creates your own sub-organization and a default wallet with a Solana, an EVM and a Cardano account.
The app signs a who-am-I request with your passkey and sends it to the ZyroPay API.
The API forwards that request to Turnkey unchanged, and Turnkey confirms who you are.
On first login the API reads your sub-org and refuses to continue unless your passkey user is its only root.
steps.ref: ARCHITECTURE.md §2.1 step 3; ADR-001 D1; SECURITY.md T14

steps.text: The API saves your account and wallet addresses and stores only hashes of your new session tokens.
The app gets a short-lived access token and a rotating refresh token, and you are in.
The agent finds ZyroPay's MCP server and identifies itself with a client metadata document, or registers if it cannot.
It starts an OAuth 2.1 sign-in with PKCE, bound to ZyroPay's single MCP resource.
The MCP worker asks the API for a pending connection and shows you a short code like ABCD-1234.
You enter the code in the ZyroPay app and see the agent's name and where it will redirect.
You pick which wallets and networks it may use and approve the connection.
The new agent starts in Always Ask, with spending disabled, zero limits and no protocols.
The MCP worker sees the approval and completes the sign-in for that one agent.
The agent receives a 15-minute access token and a rotating refresh token, stored only as hashes on ZyroPay's side.
The agent calls the send tool with a recipient, amount and an idempotency key.
The MCP server passes the request to the API, which checks the agent is still active.
The API validates the details, builds the payment terms and fingerprints them with a hash.
It values the payment in USD, rounding up, and treats a missing price as no valuation.
steps.ref: API.md Implementation notes: Validate + value; SECURITY.md C5

steps.text: Under a row lock, the policy engine checks the agent's rules against what is already spent and reserved, and decides it needs your approval.
The request waits in PENDING_APPROVAL and you get a push notification with no amounts in it.
You review the recipient and amount in the app and approve with your passkey.
The API checks the hash and that your signed request is byte-for-byte the reviewed transaction.
steps.ref: API.md Implementation notes: Approve = sign; SECURITY.md C7

steps.text: The request moves to SIGNING first, then the API forwards your passkey-signed request to Turnkey.
The signed transaction is checked again, broadcast, and settled into the ledger when the chain confirms it.
You switch an agent to Autonomous, and the API creates a signing key and returns only its public half.
Your passkey creates a limited, non-root signer user in your Turnkey sub-org for that key.
Your passkey also approves Turnkey rules that limit that signer to allowed chains, allowlisted recipients and per-transaction caps.
Later the agent asks to send a native-token payment to an allowlisted recipient.
The policy engine checks USD and daily or monthly limits against spent plus reserved, then reserves the amount.
The approved request goes to the execute job, which re-checks that it is unexpired and the agent is still autonomous.
The API signs with the delegated key, and Turnkey only allows it inside the rules you set.
steps.ref: API.md Implementation notes: Autonomous; ADR-001 D6

steps.text: The signed bytes are checked against the reviewed bytes and broadcast.
steps.ref: API.md Implementation notes: Broadcast; SECURITY.md C7

steps.text: When the chain confirms, the reservation becomes a ledger entry and you get a notification.
steps.ref: API.md Implementation notes: Confirm; ARCHITECTURE.md §2.5 step 6

flows.title: A hijacked agent tries to drain your wallet

steps.text: A prompt-injected agent asks to send a large amount to an attacker's address.
The MCP server cannot sign anything; it can only turn the call into a request, and tool results reach the agent marked as untrusted data.
The policy engine denies a recipient that is not allowed, or requires your approval, because agents start in Always Ask.
Many requests fired at once cannot add up past a limit, because each counts spent plus reserved under a row lock.
If approval is needed, you see the real recipient and amount in the app and can simply reject it.
If anyone swaps the recipient or amount after you approve, the hash changes and the old approval no longer applies.
A signed transaction that is not byte-for-byte the reviewed one is refused, and a mismatch after signing fails the request before broadcast.
steps.ref: SECURITY.md C7; API.md Implementation notes: Broadcast

steps.text: Even in Autonomous mode with a compromised server, Turnkey's rules block payments to recipients outside the allowlist or above the per-transaction cap.
You revoke the agent, which cancels its pending requests, releases its reservations and revokes its tokens at once.
steps.ref: ADR-001 D8; MCP.md Server guide §5 Revocation
